title: Replication: master-slave (read replicas), master-master (conflict resolution needed), replication lag, failover.
keyPoints: Master-slave replication has one primary for all writes and read-only replicas that scale read-heavy workloads.
Replication lag is the delay before a write on the primary appears on a replica, causing read-your-own-write anomalies.
Route a user's read to the primary right after their own write to guarantee they see their change immediately.
Master-master lets multiple nodes accept writes but introduces conflicts; dangerous for money due to conflicting balance writes.
Failover promotes the most up-to-date replica to primary and fences off the old primary to prevent split-brain.
Asynchronous replication risks losing recently acknowledged writes on failover; synchronous replication protects them at higher latency.
For banking, resolve the async-vs-sync trade-off toward durability because losing an acknowledged transaction is worse than slower writes.

s1_definition.oneliner: Copy data to replicas for read scale and availability; master-slave has one writer, master-master has many writers needing conflict resolution, replicas lag, and failover promotes a replica when the primary dies.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Replication** : copying data from one database to one or more others to improve read scalability, availability, and durability.
- **Master-slave (primary-replica)** : a single primary accepts writes and replicates to read-only replicas that serve reads.
- **Master-master** : multiple nodes accept writes and must resolve conflicts when concurrent writes touch the same data.
- **Replication lag** : the delay before a write on the primary appears on a replica.
- **Failover** : promoting a replica to primary when the primary fails, requiring detection, promotion, and fencing.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India keeps one official master ledger where all changes are written, and several photocopies that tellers across branches read from so they do not crowd the master. The copies lag the master by a tiny moment. If the master ledger is destroyed, one photocopy is promoted to become the new official master. If instead two branches could both write to their own copies, they might record conflicting changes to the same account, and the bank would need rules to reconcile them.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Replication copies data from one database to others to improve read scalability, availability, and durability. The pattern I reach for first in banking is master-slave: a single primary accepts all writes and streams its change log to read-only replicas, and I spread reads across those replicas. This fits banking perfectly because the traffic is overwhelmingly reads.

The reality I always address is replication lag. With asynchronous replication the write is acknowledged as soon as the primary commits, which is fast but means a replica can be briefly behind, causing a read-your-own-writes anomaly. I handle this by routing a user's read to the primary right after they write, so Rajesh always sees his new balance immediately.

Master-master replication improves write availability but introduces conflicts when two nodes modify the same row. For money this is dangerous because conflicting balance writes are unacceptable, so a bank almost always keeps a single writer per piece of data.

Failover is the final piece: when the primary fails, promote the most up-to-date replica, redirect writes, and fence the old primary to prevent split-brain. The senior trade-off is that async replication risks losing recently acknowledged writes during failover, while sync replication protects them at higher latency. For banking I resolve toward durability, because losing an acknowledged transaction is far worse than a slightly slower write.

Remember one sentence: replicate for read scale and availability, route reads-after-writes to the primary to avoid staleness, and resolve the async-vs-sync trade-off toward durability for money.
